answers.answer: Use the {charity.*} helpers with no arguments. For campaign progress use {charity.name}, {charity.link}, {charity.raised}, {charity.target}, {charity.percent} and {charity.bar}. For donations use {charity.donations.count} and {charity.donations.latest}. Type each one exactly as shown.
answers.quote: None of these helpers takes an input, so type each one exactly as shown.

answers.answer: You need to know how to use braces in a reply, from the Variables and templates page. The bot also needs the Twitch permission channel:read:charity. You grant it under Settings, then Integrations, with Grant permissions, while you are signed in to Twitch as the streamer's own account. Both needs are stated near the top of the page.
answers.quote: To read your campaign, the bot needs your Twitch permission channel:read:charity.

answers.answer: Success has two signs. After you approve on Twitch, the notice title says the permissions were granted. After that, the helpers show values instead of their braces. If a helper prints its braces, the table lists three causes in order: the permission is missing, no campaign is running, or Twitch did not answer.
answers.quote: After you approve on Twitch, the notice stays and its title reads “Permissions granted. Twitch now lets the bot use them.”

answers.answer: Use {charity.name}: {charity.raised} of {charity.target} {charity.bar}. Thank you, {charity.donations.latest}! for the progress and the latest donation. Before the first donation, {charity.donations.latest} prints as typed, so leave out the thank-you until a donation comes in. With no active campaign, every charity helper prints as typed, so use the command only on charity streams.
answers.quote: With no campaign running, every helper in the reply prints as typed, so use the command only on your charity streams.

answers.answer: The page tells me to type my charity command in chat before a charity stream. That comes before it shows any charity command, and the !charity example only appears at the end, so I had to read ahead to know which command it means. The cost is a small detour, and it does not block the task.
answers.quote: So type your charity command once in your channel’s chat before a charity stream, and then look at Needs attention.

answers.answer: Three failure messages in a row, each quoted in full, are long to hear read aloud. Each one points to the same action, choosing Grant permissions again. The cost is listening time, not lost meaning.
answers.quote: The code ran out: “The code ran out before it was used. Grant the permissions again for a new code.”

warning_review.reason: Five short sentences, but they all serve the Grant step: the notice wording the reader will see, that a Moderator or up can start the grant, and that the streamer's own Twitch account must approve. This access requirement comes before the numbered steps, as voice.md asks, and no sentence is generic teaching the reader does not need.

Five short sentences on how amounts look: the symbol and decimals, the Language setting that controls grouping, the English fallback, and the currency-code case. Each is one fact the reader needs to match the example output to their channel, and the pointer to Bot basics and personality is the only place that setting is explained. Length alone is not a defect.
